analysis.one_liner: Charges a rising fee on fossil fuel carbon pollution and returns most of the money as quarterly rebates to adults.
analysis.headline: Durbin's carbon fee-and-dividend bill, starting at $75 per ton and rising $10 a year, sits in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors and no action since its September 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill puts a fee on the carbon pollution from coal, oil, and natural gas, starting at $75 per ton in 2027 and rising each year, with extra increases if emissions miss targets. The money mostly goes back out as quarterly cash payments to every adult in the country, phasing out for individuals making over $75,000 or couples over $150,000. The rest funds a new Climate Change Finance Corporation that finances clean energy projects, transition help for coal and oil communities, and payments to farmers who cut emissions. A border charge applies the same cost to imported steel, cement, and fuels so U.S. producers aren't undercut.
analysis.who_benefits: Most households below the income thresholds: because the fee is charged upstream to fuel producers and most of the revenue is paid back as equal quarterly rebates to every adult, a typical lower- and middle-income household receives more in rebates than it pays in higher fuel prices. It also benefits workers in clean energy and communities hit by coal plant and refinery closures, which get job training, cleanup, and resiliency funding, and it benefits farmers through transition payments for climate-smart practices.

how_it_helps.text: Every adult with a valid SSN and U.S. residence gets quarterly carbon fee rebate payments, tax-free and not counted as income for federal benefits, with payments phasing out above $75,000 individual / $150,000 joint income.

The fee starts at $75 per ton of CO2-equivalent in 2027, rises $10 per year, and the annual increase jumps to $15-$25 if the country misses its emissions targets; fee revenue is deposited in a dedicated America's Clean Future Fund.

In the first ten years, 75 percent of fund money goes to the rebates, 15 percent to the new Climate Change Finance Corporation, and 10 percent to transition assistance for carbon-intensive communities; at least 40 percent of grant funds must benefit environmental justice and low-income communities.

A border adjustment charges imported steel, aluminum, cement, glass, chemicals, and fuels an equivalent fee and refunds the fee on exports, so domestic manufacturers are not at a disadvantage against countries with no carbon price.
All construction on funded projects must pay Davis-Bacon prevailing wages and use American-made iron, steel, and manufactured goods.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, refiners, and importers pay the fee directly and pass much of it to consumers through higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices. Households above the rebate phaseout thresholds pay in without getting the full rebate back, and energy-intensive manufacturers face fees on their industrial emissions, softened by border refunds and import charges.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and their customers

drawbacks.text: Energy prices rise immediately while rebates phase in, and rural and long-commute households that drive a lot or heat with fuel oil could pay more in fuel costs than they receive back, since everyone gets the same flat rebate regardless of fuel use.

Rebates disappear entirely for households above $75,000 (individual) or $150,000 (joint) modified adjusted gross income, and phase out at 5 percent per $1,000 over the threshold, so many middle-income households bear the fee with little offset.

The bill appropriates large sums up front regardless of fee collections: $37.5 billion in each of fiscal 2026 and 2027 for the initial rebates, $7.5 billion a year for the Climate Change Finance Corporation, and $5 billion a year for community transition grants, plus roughly $7.1 billion a year of general Treasury money routed into the fund for its first 14 years.

A $75-per-ton fee would be among the highest carbon prices in the world and roughly triple the price of a metric ton of coal's emissions impact on electricity bills; even supporters must acknowledge the transition shock to coal regions and energy-heavy industries, which is why the bill pairs it with transition aid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The fee-and-dividend structure is one of the more progressive ways to price carbon: the flat adult rebate means most lower- and middle-income households come out ahead on net, and the border adjustment plus transition grants address the two strongest fair objections (industry leakage and coal/oil community decline). The real costs are the transition shock to energy prices, the exposure of rural high-fuel-use households, the phaseout that leaves upper-middle households paying without full rebates, and the creation of a large new spending agency whose loan guarantees carry default risk. Whether the design's benefits outweigh those costs is genuinely debatable, but the bill was written to blunt the usual objections, and it still attracted no cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Durbin introduced the bill on September 4, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
The bill has zero cosponsors, so no other senator has put their name on it.
No further action has been taken since the referral; the Finance Committee has not scheduled a markup or vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: fossil fuel producers face no carbon fee, and no household has received any rebate, because the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo: fossil fuel producers pay nothing

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Only one Democrat sponsored the bill and no senator from either party cosponsored it, and no votes have been recorded, so the partisan shape is unknown.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and importers
industries.note: These companies pay the $75-per-ton fee directly on fuels they sell, escalating each year, and fees on methane leaks and industrial emissions after 2028. Their financial interest in blocking the fee runs against the public's interest in emissions cuts funded by rebates.

industries.industry: Clean energy and clean vehicle industries
industries.note: The Climate Change Finance Corporation gives grants and 75 percent loan guarantees for solar, wind, geothermal, storage, EV charging, hydrogen, and carbon capture projects, prioritizing high-risk projects private capital avoids. Rising fossil fuel prices also make clean alternatives more competitive.

industries.industry: Banks, credit unions, and green banks
industries.note: The bill routes clean energy financing through eligible lenders by guaranteeing 75 percent of qualifying loans and funding state and local green banks directly, making these lenders the permanent channel for public climate finance and charging borrowers guarantee fees up to 3.5 percent.

industries.industry: Carbon-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals, glass)
industries.note: They pay fees on industrial process emissions after 2028, but the border adjustment refunds fees on exports and charges equivalent fees on imported carbon-intensive products, protecting them from competitors in countries without a carbon price.

Farmers pay more for diesel and fertilizer but can receive decarbonization transition payments for measurable climate-smart practices, with priority consideration for underserved and limited-resource producers.

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress is still in session, so the bill is technically alive, but with a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no Finance Committee action nearly a full session after introduction, it follows the well-worn path of carbon tax bills: it will almost certainly die quietly in committee unless a broader revenue or climate negotiation picks it up, which the current Senate composition makes unlikely.
